summary:
Allwork.Space republishes a FlexJobs press release on its Job Search Pulse Report, which surveyed 2,142 U.S. workers between August 21-30, 2026 about job search behavior. The headline finding: 61% of U.S. workers say they "doomscroll" job listings at least weekly, including 28% who do so daily or almost daily. Another 16% browse up to a few times a month, 11% less than monthly, and 12% never.

Most of this browsing is low intent. 61% spend up to an hour scrolling listings with no intention of applying; 15% spend one to two hours, 8% more than two hours, and only 16% spend 15 minutes or less. The leading motivation is curiosity about available opportunities (53%), followed by dissatisfaction with the current job (15%), job security concerns (10%), checking salaries (9%), seeing a career-related social post (6%), and habit or boredom (5%).

Outcomes are mostly negative. 42% say they rarely or never apply to a role they find, and 32% apply only sometimes. 42% report feeling more stressed, overwhelmed, or uncertain about their career afterward, versus 22% who feel motivated, optimistic, or committed to their current role.

Keith Spencer, FlexJobs Career Expert, says brief browsing can provide a sense of stability in an uncertain market, but that social media has turned an intentional process into a compulsive habit, and scrolling without goals or guardrails leaves workers anxious and fatigued.

On converting scrollers to applicants, workers cite more transparent salary information (24%), easier ways to judge fit (20%), clearer job requirements (18%), fewer duplicate or outdated postings (5%), and clearer hiring timelines (4%).

Methodology notes a skew: 71% women, 42% Gen X, 54% experienced level, recruited via FlexJobs social media and newsletters using SurveyMonkey.
